contenido: 1. The mission of Christ the Redeemer, entrusted to the Church, is still far from being fulfilled. At the end of the second millennium after his coming, a global look at humanity shows that this mission is still in its beginnings and that we must commit all our energies to its service. It is the Holy Spirit who prompts us to announce the great works of God: «Preaching the Gospel is no reason for glory for me; It is rather a duty that rests upon me: And woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel! » (1 Cor 9, 16).

2. The missionary fruits of the Council are already many: local Churches provided with their own Bishop, clergy and apostolic personnel have multiplied; a deeper insertion of Christian communities into the life of the people is being achieved; communion between the Churches leads to an effective exchange of spiritual goods and gifts; the evangelizing work of the laity is changing ecclesial life; The particular Churches are open to encounter, dialogue and collaboration with members of other Christian Churches and other religions. Above all, a new awareness is taking hold: the mission concerns all Christians, all dioceses and parishes, ecclesiastical institutions and associations.

3. All peoples, open the doors to Christ! His Gospel does not take away anything from human freedom, from due respect for cultures, from all that is good in each religion. By welcoming Christ, you open yourself to the definitive Word of God, to the one in whom God has made himself fully known and to whom God himself has indicated to us the path to reach him.

4. The fundamental task of the Church in all times and particularly in ours – as I recalled in my first programmatic Encyclical – is “to direct the gaze of man, to orient the conscience and experience of all humanity towards the mystery of Christ.”4

5. Going back to the origins of the Church, we see it clearly stated that Christ is the only Savior of humanity, the only one in a position to reveal God and guide towards God. To the Jewish religious authorities who question the Apostles about Peter's healing of the cripple, he answers: "By the name of Jesus Christ, the Nazarene, whom you crucified and whom God raised from the dead; By his name and by no other does this man present himself here healthy before you... For there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved » (Act 4, 10. 12). This statement, addressed to the Sanhedrin, assumes a universal value, since for all "Jews and Gentiles" salvation can only come from Jesus Christ.

6. It is contrary to the Christian faith to introduce any separation between the Word and Jesus Christ. Saint John clearly states that the Word, who "was in the beginning with God", is the same one who "became flesh" (Jn 1, 2.14). Jesus is the incarnate Word, one person and inseparable: Jesus cannot be separated from Christ, nor can we speak of a "Jesus of history", which would be different from the "Christ of faith". The Church knows and confesses Jesus as "the Christ, the Son of the living God" (Mt 16, 16). Christ is none other than Jesus of Nazareth, and this is the Word of God made man for the salvation of all. In Christ "all the fullness of divinity resides bodily" (Col 2, 9) and "from his fullness we have all received" (Jn 1, 16). The “Only Son, who is in the bosom of the Father” (Jn 1, 18), is the “Son of his love, in whom we have redemption. For God was pleased to make all fullness reside in him, and to reconcile through him and for him all things, pacifying, through the blood of his cross, what is on earth and in heaven" (Col 1, 13-14.19-20). It is precisely this unique singularity of Christ that gives him an absolute and universal meaning, which is why, while he is in history, he is the center and the end of it: 7 "I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End" (Ap 22, 13).

7. The urgency of missionary activity springs from the radical newness of life, brought by Christ and lived by his disciples. This new life is a gift from God, and man is asked to welcome and develop it, if he wants to fulfill himself according to his integral vocation, in accordance with Christ. The New Testament is a hymn to new life for those who believe in Christ and live in his Church. Salvation in Christ, witnessed and announced by the Church, is God's self-communication: «It is love, which not only creates good, but also makes us participate in the very life of God: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Indeed, he who loves desires to give of himself."9

8. In the modern world there is a tendency to reduce man to a mere horizontal dimension. But what does man become without openness to the Absolute? The answer is found not only in the experience of each man, but also in the history of humanity with the blood shed in the name of ideologies and political regimes that have wanted to build a "new humanity" without God.11

9. The first beneficiary of salvation is the Church. Christ has acquired it with his blood (cf. Act 20, 28) and has made it his collaborator in the work of universal salvation. Indeed, Christ lives in her; is her husband; encourages its growth; Through it he fulfills his mission.

10. The universality of salvation does not mean that it is granted only to those who, explicitly, believe in Christ and have entered the Church. If it is intended for all, salvation must truly be available to all. But it is evident that, both today and in the past, many men do not have the possibility of knowing or accepting the revelation of the Gospel and of entering the Church. They live in sociocultural conditions that do not allow it and, in many cases, they have been educated in other religious traditions. For them, the salvation of Christ is accessible by virtue of the grace that, although having a mysterious relationship with the Church, does not formally introduce them into it, but rather illuminates them appropriately in their interior and environmental situation. This grace comes from Christ; It is the fruit of his sacrifice and is communicated by the Holy Spirit: it allows each one to reach salvation through their free collaboration.

11. What, then, can we say about the objections already mentioned about the mission ad gentes? With full respect for all beliefs and sensitivities, above all we must simply affirm our faith in Christ, the only savior of man; faith received as a gift that comes from Above, without merit on our part. We say with Saint Paul: "I am not ashamed of the Gospel, which is a power from God for the salvation of everyone who believes" (Rom 1, 16). The Christian martyrs of all times – including ours – have given and continue to give their lives to bear witness to this faith before men, convinced that every man needs Jesus Christ, who has conquered sin and death, and has reconciled men with God.

12. « God rich in mercy is the one whom Jesus Christ has revealed to us as Father; precisely his Son, in himself, has manifested it to us and made it known to us. "21 He wrote this at the beginning of the Encyclical Dives in Misericordia, showing how Christ is the revelation and incarnation of the Father's mercy. Salvation consists of believing and accepting the mystery of the Father and his love, which is manifested and given in Jesus through the Spirit. This is how the Kingdom of God is fulfilled, already prepared by the Old Alliance, carried out by Christ and in Christ, and announced to all people by the Church, which strives and prays so that it reaches its fullness in a perfect and definitive way.

13. Jesus of Nazareth brings God's plan to fulfillment. After having received the Holy Spirit in baptism, he manifests his messianic vocation: he travels around Galilee proclaiming «the Good News of God: "The time is fulfilled and the Kingdom is near; convert and believe in the Good News" » (Mc 1, 14-15; cf. Mt 4, 17; Lc 4, 43). The proclamation and establishment of the Kingdom of God are the object of his mission: "For to this end I have been sent" (Lc 4, 43). But there is something more: Jesus in person is the "Good News", as he himself affirms at the beginning of his mission in the synagogue of Nazareth, applying the words of Isaiah regarding the Anointed One, sent by the Spirit of the Lord (cf. Lc. 4, 14-21). Since he is the "Good News", there is in Christ full identity between message and messenger, between saying, acting and being. Its strength, the secret of the effectiveness of its action, consists in total identification with the message it announces; He proclaims the "Good News" not only with what he says or does, but also with what he is.
14. Jesus progressively reveals the characteristics and demands of the Kingdom through his words, his works and his person.

15. The Kingdom tends to transform human relationships and is realized progressively, as men learn to love, forgive and serve each other. Jesus refers to the entire law, centering it on the commandment of love (cf. Mt 22, 34-40); Lk 10, 25-28). Before leaving his people he gives them a "new commandment": "That you love one another as I have loved you" (Jn 15, 12; cf. 13, 34). The love with which Jesus loved the world finds its supreme expression in the gift of his life for men (cf. Jn 15, 13), thus manifesting the love that the Father has for the world (cf. Jn 3, 16). Therefore the nature of the Kingdom is the communion of all human beings with each other and with God.

16. By resurrecting Jesus from the dead, God has defeated death and in him has definitively inaugurated his Kingdom. During his earthly life Jesus is the prophet of the Kingdom and, after his passion, resurrection and ascension to heaven, he participates in the power of God and his dominion over the world (cf. Mt 28, 18; Act 2, 36; Ef 1, 18-31). The resurrection confers universal scope on Christ's message, his action and his entire mission. The disciples realize that the Kingdom is already present in the person of Jesus and is gradually being established in man and in the world through a mysterious link with him.

17. Today there is a lot of talk about the Kingdom, but not always in tune with the feelings of the Church. In fact, there are conceptions of salvation and mission that we can call "anthropocentric", in the reductive sense of the term, as they are centered around the earthly needs of man. In this perspective, the Kingdom tends to become a fully human and secularized reality, in which only the programs and struggles for socioeconomic, political and cultural liberation count, but with horizons closed to the transcendent. While not denying that there are also values ​​to be promoted at that level, however, such a conception is reduced to the confines of a kingdom of man, amputated in its authentic and profound dimensions, and is easily translated into one of the ideologies that look to merely earthly progress. The Kingdom of God, on the other hand, “is not of this world, it is not of here” (Jn 18, 36).
18. Now, this is not the Kingdom of God that we know from Revelation, which cannot be separated either from Christ or from the Church.

19. It is in this overall vision that the reality of the Kingdom is understood. Certainly, this requires the promotion of human goods and values ​​that can well be called "evangelical", because they are closely linked to the Good News. But this promotion, which the Church also feels deeply within itself, should not be separated or opposed to other fundamental tasks, such as the proclamation of Christ and his Gospel, the foundation and development of communities that act among men as the living image of the Kingdom. With this we do not have to be afraid of falling into a form of "ecclesiocentrism." Paul VI, who affirmed the existence of "a deep bond between Christ, the Church and evangelization,"26 also said that the Church "is not an end for itself, but fervently eager to be all of Christ, in Christ and for Christ, and all equally of men, among men and for men."27

20. The Church is effectively and concretely at the service of the Kingdom. It is, above all, through the advertisement that calls for conversion; This is the first and fundamental service for the coming of the Kingdom in people and in human society. Eschatological salvation begins, from now on, with the newness of life in Christ: "To all who received him he gave the power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name" (Jn 1, 12).

21. « At the culminating moment of Jesus' messianic mission, the Holy Spirit is present in the paschal mystery with all his divine subjectivity: as the one who must continue the saving work, based on the sacrifice of the cross. Without a doubt this work is entrusted by Jesus to men: to the Apostles and the Church. However, in these men and through them, the Holy Spirit continues to be the transcendent protagonist of the realization of this work in the spirit of man and in the history of the world. "31

22. All the evangelists, when narrating the meeting of the Risen Lord with the Apostles, conclude with the missionary mandate: «All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations. Know that I am with you always until the end of the world » (Mt 28, 18-20; cf. Mc 16, 15-18; Lc 24, 46-49; Jn 20, 21-23).

23. The various forms of the "missionary mandate" have common points and also characteristic accentuations. Two elements, however, are found in all versions. First of all, the universal dimension of the task entrusted to the Apostles: "To all nations" (Mt 28, 19); « throughout the world... to all creation » (Mc 16, 15); «to all nations» (Act 1, 8). Secondly, the certainty given by the Lord that in this task they will not be alone, but that they will receive the strength and means to carry out their mission. In this is the presence and power of the Spirit, and the assistance of Jesus: "They went out to preach everywhere, the Lord working with them" (Mc 16, 20).

24. The mission of the Church, like that of Jesus, is the work of God or, as Luke often says, the work of the Spirit. After the resurrection and ascension of Jesus, the Apostles live a profound experience that transforms them: Pentecost. The coming of the Holy Spirit turns them into witnesses or prophets (cf. Act 1, 8; 2, 17-18), instilling in them a serene audacity that drives them to transmit to others their experience of Jesus and the hope that animates them. The Spirit gives them the ability to witness to Jesus with "all freedom."33

25. The missionaries have proceeded along this line, keeping in mind the expectations and hopes, the anxieties and sufferings, the culture of the people to announce salvation in Christ. The speeches of Lystra and Athens (cf. Act 14, 11-17; 17, 22-31) are considered models for the evangelization of pagans. In them Paul "enters into dialogue" with the cultural and religious values ​​of the various peoples. To the inhabitants of Lycaonia, who practiced a cosmic-type religion, it reminds them of religious experiences that refer to the cosmos; with the Greeks he discusses philosophy and quotes their poets (cf. Act 17, 18.26-28). The God he wants to reveal is already present in his life; It is he, in fact, who created them and who mysteriously directs people and history. However, to recognize the true God, it is necessary that they abandon the false gods that they themselves have created and open themselves to the one whom God has sent to fill their ignorance and satisfy the desire of their hearts (cf. Act 17, 27-30). They are speeches that offer an example of inculturation of the Gospel.

26. The Spirit moves the group of believers to "make community", to be Church. After Peter's first announcement, on the day of Pentecost, and the conversions that followed, the first community was formed (cf. Act 2, 42-47; 4, 32-35).

27. The Acts indicate that the mission, directed first to Israel and then to the people, develops on many levels. First of all, there is the group of the Twelve who, as a single body led by Peter, proclaim the Good News. Then there is the community of believers who, with their way of living and acting, bear witness to the Lord and convert the pagans (cf. Act 2, 46-47). There are also special envoys, destined to announce the Gospel. And so, the Christian community of Antioch sends its members on mission: after having fasted, prayed and celebrated the Eucharist, this community perceives that the Holy Spirit has chosen Paul and Barnabas to be sent (cf. Act 13, 1-4). In its origins, therefore, the mission is considered a community commitment and a responsibility of the local Church, which needs precisely "missionaries" to launch itself into new frontiers. Along with those sent there were others who spontaneously witnessed the novelty that had transformed their lives and then connected the communities in formation with the apostolic Church.

28. The Spirit manifests himself in a particular way in the Church and in its members; However, its presence and action are universal, without any limit of space or time.35 The Second Vatican Council remembers the action of the Spirit in the heart of man, through the "seeds of the Word", even in religious initiatives, in the efforts of human activity aimed at truth, good and God.36

29. Thus the Spirit who "breaths where he wills" (Jn 3, 8) and "was already working in the world even before Christ was glorified,"43 who "fills the world and holds everything together, who knows everything that is spoken" (Sab 1, 7), leads us to open our gaze more to consider his present action in all times and places.44 It is a call that I myself have made repeatedly and that has guided me in my encounters with the most diverse peoples. The relationship of the Church with other religions is guided by a double respect: "Respect for man in his search for answers to the most profound questions of life, and respect for the action of the Spirit in man."45 The interreligious meeting of Assisi, excluding any equivocal interpretation, sought to reaffirm my conviction that "every authentic prayer is moved by the Holy Spirit, who is mysteriously present in the heart of each person.46

30. Our time, with humanity in movement and search, demands a new impulse in the missionary activity of the Church. The horizons and possibilities of the mission are broadening, and we Christians are called to apostolic courage, based on trust in the Spirit. He is the protagonist of the mission!

31. The Lord Jesus sent his Apostles to all people and towns, and to all places on earth. Through the Apostles the Church received a universal mission, which knows no boundaries and concerns salvation in all its integrity, in accordance with the fullness of life that Christ came to bring (cf. Jn 10,10); It has been sent "to manifest and communicate the charity of God to all men and peoples."49

32. Today we find ourselves facing a quite diversified and changing religious situation; the towns are on the move; Social and religious realities, which once were clear and defined, today are transformed into complex situations. It is enough to think about some phenomena, such as urban planning, mass migrations, the movement of refugees, the de-Christianization of countries of ancient Christianity, the powerful influence of the Gospel and its values ​​in nations with a very large non-Christian majority, the swarming of messianisms and religious sects. It is such a disruption of religious and social situations that it is difficult to concretely apply certain distinctions and ecclesiastical categories to which we were already accustomed. Before the Council it was already said of some metropolises or Christian lands that they had become "mission countries"; certainly the situation has not improved in successive years.

33. The differences regarding the activity within this mission of the Church arise not from reasons intrinsic to the mission itself, but from the diverse circumstances in which it develops.51 Looking at the world today, from the point of view of evangelization, three situations can be distinguished.

34. Specific missionary activity, or mission ad gentes, has as its recipients "the peoples or human groups that do not yet believe in Christ", "those who are far from Christ", among whom the Church "has not yet taken root",53 and whose culture has not yet been influenced by the Gospel.54 This activity is distinguished from other ecclesiastical activities, because it is directed at non-Christian groups and environments, due to the absence or insufficiency of the evangelical proclamation and the ecclesiastical presence. Therefore, it is characterized as the task of announcing Christ and his Gospel, edifying the local Church, and promoting the values ​​of the Kingdom. The peculiarity of this mission ad gentes is the fact that it is addressed to "non-Christians." Therefore, we must prevent this "more specifically missionary responsibility that Jesus has entrusted and daily entrusts again to his Church",55 from becoming a weak reality within the global mission of the People of God and, consequently, neglected or forgotten.

35. The mission ad gentes has before it an immense task that is by no means on the verge of extinction. On the contrary, whether from a numerical point of view due to demographic increase, or from a sociocultural point of view due to the emergence of new relationships, communications and changes in situations, it seems destined for even broader horizons. The task of announcing Jesus Christ to all peoples appears immense and disproportionate to the human forces of the Church.

36. There is also no shortage of internal difficulties for the People of God, which are certainly the most painful. My predecessor Paul VI pointed out, first of all, "the lack of fervor, all the more serious because it comes from within." This lack of fervor is manifested in fatigue and disillusionment, in accommodation to the environment and in disinterest, and above all in the lack of joy and hope. "56 Great obstacles to the missionary activity of the Church are also the past and present divisions among Christians,57 the de-Christianization of Christian countries, the decrease in vocations to the apostolate, the anti-testimonies of faithful who in their lives do not follow the example of Christ. But one of the most serious reasons for the lack of interest in missionary commitment is the indifferent mentality, widely spread, unfortunately, even among Christians, often rooted in incorrect theological conceptions and marked by a religious relativism that ends up thinking that "one religion is worth the other." We can add - as the Pontiff himself said - that there is also no shortage of "pretexts that seem to oppose evangelization." The most insidious are certainly those for whose justification certain teachings of the Council are used. "58

37. The mission ad gentes by virtue of the universal mandate of Christ knows no limits. However, several areas in which it is carried out can be outlined, so that a real vision of the situation can be had.

38. Our time is dramatic and at the same time fascinating. While on the one hand men give the impression of pursuing material prosperity and immersing themselves more and more in consumer materialism, on the other hand, they manifest the anguished search for meaning, the need for interiority, the desire to learn new forms and modes of concentration and prayer. Not only in cultures steeped in religiosity, but also in secularized societies, the spiritual dimension of life is sought as an antidote to dehumanization. This so-called "religious return" phenomenon is not without ambiguity, but it also contains an invitation. The Church has an immense spiritual heritage to offer humanity: in Christ, who proclaims himself "the Way, the Truth and the Life" (Jn 14, 6). It is the Christian way to encounter God, to prayer, asceticism, the discovery of the meaning of life. This is also an areopagus that must be evangelized.

39. All forms of missionary activity are marked by the awareness of promoting the freedom of man, announcing Jesus Christ to him. The Church must be faithful to Christ, of which it is the Body and continuator of his mission. It is necessary that she walk “on the same path as Christ; that is, along the path of poverty, obedience, service and self-immolation until death, from which he emerged victorious through his resurrection. "63 The Church, then, has the duty to do everything possible to develop its mission in the world and reach all peoples; He also has the right that God has given him to carry out his plan. Religious freedom, sometimes still limited or restricted, is the premise and guarantee of all the freedoms that ensure the common good of individuals and peoples. It is to be desired that authentic religious freedom be granted to everyone everywhere; To this end, the Church deploys its work in different countries, especially in those with a Catholic majority, where it has greater weight. This is not a problem of majority or minority religion, but rather an inalienable right of every human person.

40. Missionary activity still represents the greatest challenge for the Church today. As the end of the second millennium of the Redemption approaches, it is increasingly evident that the people who have not yet received the first announcement of Christ are the majority of humanity. THE balance of missionary activity in modern times is certainly positive: the Church has been founded on all Continents; What's more, today the majority of the faithful and the particular Churches are no longer in old Europe but in the Continents that the missionaries have opened to the faith.

41. "Missionary activity is, ultimately, the manifestation of God's purpose, or epiphany, and its realization in the world and in history, in which God, through mission, openly perfects the history of salvation."68 What path does the Church follow to achieve this result?

42. Contemporary man believes witnesses more than teachers;69 he believes more in experience than in doctrine, in life and facts than in theories. The testimony of Christian life is the first and irreplaceable form of the mission: Christ, whose mission we are continuers, is the "Witness" par excellence (Ap 1, 5; 3, 14) and the model of Christian testimony. The Holy Spirit accompanies the path of the Church and associates it with the testimony that it gives of Christ (cf. Jn 15, 26-27).

43. The Christian and the Christian communities live deeply inserted in the life of their respective peoples and are a sign of the Gospel even through fidelity to their homeland, to their people, to the national culture, but always with the freedom that Christ has brought. Christianity is open to universal brotherhood, because all men are children of the same Father and brothers in Christ.

44. THE announcement has permanent priority in the mission: the Church cannot escape the explicit command of Christ; cannot deprive men of the "Good News" that they are loved and saved by God. «Evangelization must also always contain – as the base, center and at the same time the culmination of its dynamism – a clear proclamation that in Jesus Christ, salvation is offered to all men, as a gift of the grace and mercy of God. "72 All forms of missionary activity are oriented towards this proclamation that reveals and introduces the mystery hidden in the centuries and revealed in Christ (cf. Ef 3, 3-9; Col 1, 25-29), which is the center of the mission and the life of the Church, as the basis of all evangelization.

45. Since it is made in union with the entire ecclesial community, the announcement is never a personal event. The missionary is present and acts by virtue of a mandate received and, even if he is alone, he is united by invisible but profound ties to the evangelizing activity of the entire Church.76 The listeners, sooner or later, glimpse through him the community that has sent him and sustains him.

46. The announcement of the Word of God tends to Christian conversion, that is, to full and sincere adhesion to Christ and his Gospel through faith. Conversion is a gift from God, the work of the Trinity; It is the Spirit who opens the doors of hearts, so that men can believe in the Lord and "confess" Him (cf. 1 Cor 12, 3). Of those who approach him by faith, Jesus says: "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him" (Jn 6, 44).

47. The Apostles, moved by the Holy Spirit, invited everyone to change their lives, to convert and to receive baptism. Immediately after the event of Pentecost, Peter speaks persuasively to the crowd «When they heard this, they said with a heavy heart to Peter and the other Apostles: "What shall we do, brothers?" Peter answered them: "Repent and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of your sins; and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit" (Act 2, 37-38). And he baptized that day about three thousand people. Peter himself, after the healing of the cripple, speaks to the crowd and repeats: "Repent, therefore, and convert, so that your sins may be blotted out" (Act 3, 19).

48. Conversion and baptism introduce into the Church, where it already exists, or require the constitution of new communities that confess Jesus Savior and Lord. This is part of God's plan, which pleased "to call men to participate in his life not only individually, without any mutual connection between them, but to constitute them into a people in which his children, who were dispersed, are gathered in unity."78

49. It is necessary, above all, to try to establish Christian communities in each place that are an "exponent of the presence of God in the world" 80 and grow until they become Churches. Despite the large number of dioceses, there are still large areas in which local Churches either do not exist at all or are insufficient in relation to the extent of the territory and the density and variety of the population; There remains a great work to be done to establish and develop the Church. This phase of ecclesial history, called plantatio Ecclesiae, is not finished; What's more, in many human groups it has yet to begin.

50. This request will constitute a motive and a stimulus for renewed ecumenical action. The existing links between ecumenical activity and missionary activity make it necessary to consider two concomitant factors. On the one hand, it must be recognized that "the division of Christians harms the most holy cause of preaching the Gospel to every creature and closes the doors of faith to many."81 The fact that the Good News of reconciliation is preached by Christians divided among themselves weakens their testimony, and for this reason it is urgent to work for the unity of Christians, so that missionary activity is more incisive. At the same time, we must not forget that the very efforts for unity constitute in themselves a sign of the work of reconciliation that God carries out in our midst.

51. A phenomenon of rapid expansion in the young Churches, sometimes promoted by the Bishops and their Conferences as a priority option for pastoral care, are the "base ecclesial communities" (conocidas también con otros nombres), which are giving positive proof as centers of Christian formation and missionary irradiation. These are groups of Christians at the family level or in a restricted area, which meet for prayer, reading Scripture, catechesis, to share human and ecclesiastical problems in the face of a common commitment. They are a sign of vitality of the Church, an instrument of formation and evangelization, a valid starting point for a new society founded on the "civilization of Love."

52. When developing its missionary activity among people, the Church encounters diverse cultures and is involved in the process of inculturation. This is a demand that has marked its entire historical path, but today it is particularly acute and urgent.

53. Missionaries, coming from other Churches and countries, must insert themselves into the sociocultural world of those to whom they are sent, overcoming the conditions of their own environment of origin. Thus, they must learn the language of the region where they work, know the most significant expressions of that culture, discovering its values ​​through direct experience. Only with this knowledge will missionaries be able to bring the knowledge of the hidden mystery to the people in a credible and fruitful way (cf. Rom 16, 25-27; Ef 3, 5). For them it is certainly not about denying one's own cultural identity, but about understanding, appreciating, promoting and evangelizing that of the environment where they operate and, consequently, being in a position to truly communicate with it, assuming a lifestyle that is a sign of evangelical testimony and solidarity with the people.

54. In this regard, some indications are essential. Inculturation, in its correct process, must be guided by two principles: "compatibility with the Gospel of the various cultures to be assumed and communion with the universal Church."94 The Bishops, guardians of the "deposit of faith" will take care of fidelity and, above all, discernment,95 for which a profound balance is necessary; Indeed, there is a risk of uncritically moving from a kind of alienation from culture to an overvaluation of it, which is a product of man, consequently, marked by sin. She too must be "purified, elevated and perfected."96

55. Interreligious dialogue is part of the evangelizing mission of the Church. Understood as a method and means for mutual knowledge and enrichment, it is not in contrast to the mission ad gentes; In fact, it has special ties with it and is one of its expressions. Indeed, this mission is addressed to men who do not know Christ and his Gospel, and who for the most part belong to other religions. God calls all people to himself in Christ, wanting to communicate to them the fullness of his revelation and his love; and it continues to be present in many ways, not only in each individual but also in people through its spiritual riches, whose main and essential expression are religions, even if they contain "gaps, insufficiencies and errors."98 All of this has been widely emphasized by the Second Vatican Council and by the subsequent Magisterium, always defending that salvation comes from Christ and that dialogue does not dispense with evangelization.99

56. Dialogue is not born of a tactic or an interest, but is an activity with its own motivations, demands and dignity: it is demanded by the deep respect for everything that the Spirit has worked in man, which "blows where it wills" (Jn 3, 8).103 With this the Church tries to discover the "seeds of the Word" 104 the "sparkle of that Truth that illuminates all men",105 seeds and sparks that are found in people and in the religious traditions of humanity. Dialogue is founded on hope and charity, and will bear fruit in the Spirit. Other religions constitute a positive challenge for the Church today; In fact, they stimulate it both to discover and know the signs of the presence of Christ and the action of the Spirit, as well as to deepen its own identity and to bear witness to the integrity of Revelation, of which it is the depositary for the good of all.

57. A vast field is open to dialogue, which can take on multiple forms and expressions, from exchanges between experts of religious traditions or official representatives of the same, to collaboration for comprehensive development and the safeguarding of religious values; from the communication of the respective spiritual experiences to the so-called "dialogue of life", by which believers of the various religions witness to each other in their daily existence their own human and spiritual values, and help each other to live them to build a more just and fraternal society.

58. The mission ad gentes is deployed even today, mostly, in those southern regions of the world where action for integral development and liberation from all oppression is most urgent. The Church has always known how to arouse, in the populations it has evangelized, an impulse towards progress, and right now missionaries, more than in the past, are also known as promoters of development by governments and international experts, who marvel at the fact that notable results are achieved with limited means.

59. With the evangelical message the Church offers a liberating force and promoter of development, precisely because it leads to the conversion of heart and mentality; helps to recognize the dignity of each person; disposes to solidarity, commitment, service to brothers; inserts man into God's project, which is the construction of the Kingdom of peace and justice, starting from this life. It is the biblical perspective of the "new heavens and new earth" (cf. Is 65, 17; 2 Pe 3, 13; Ap 21, 1), which has introduced into history the stimulus and goal for the progress of humanity. The development of man comes from God, from the model of Jesus, God and man, and must lead to God.111 That is why there is a close connection between the evangelical proclamation and the promotion of man.

60. «The Church throughout the world – I said in my first pastoral visit to Brazil – wants to be the Church of the poor... it wants to extract all the truth contained in the beatitudes of Christ and especially in this first one: "Blessed are the poor in spirit...". He wants to teach this truth and wants to put it into practice, just as Jesus came to do and teach.”114

61. There is no testimony without witnesses, just as there is no mission without missionaries. To collaborate in his mission and continue his saving work, Jesus chooses and sends some people as his witnesses and Apostles: "You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth" (Act 1, 8).

62. What was done at the beginning of Christianity for the universal mission also remains valid and urgent today. The Church is missionary by its very nature since the mandate of Christ is not something contingent and external, but rather reaches to the very heart of the Church. For this reason, the entire Church and each Church is sent to the people. The younger Churches themselves, precisely "in order for this missionary zeal to flourish in the members of their homeland," must participate "as soon as possible and in fact in the universal mission of the Church, themselves sending missionaries to preach the Gospel to all parts of the world, even if they suffer from a shortage of clergy."117 Many already act in this way, and I strongly encourage them to continue.

63. Just as the risen Lord conferred on the Apostolic College headed by Peter the mandate of the universal mission, so this responsibility falls on the Episcopal College headed by the Successor of Peter.119 Aware of this responsibility, in meetings with the Bishops I feel the duty to share it, with a view to both the new evangelization and the universal mission. I have set out on the roads of the world «to announce the Gospel, to "confirm the brothers" in the faith, to console the Church, to find man. They are journeys of faith... They are so many occasions of itinerant catechesis, of evangelical proclamation for the extension, in all latitudes, of the Gospel and of the Apostolic Magisterium expanded to the current planetary spheres. "120

64. Every particular Church must open itself generously to the needs of others. Collaboration between the Churches, through real reciprocity that prepares them to give and receive, is also a source of enrichment for all and covers various sectors of ecclesial life. In this regard, the declaration of the Bishops in Puebla is exemplary: «Finally, the time has come for Latin America... to project itself beyond its own borders, ad gentes. It is true that we ourselves need missionaries. But we must give from our poverty. "126

65. Among the agents of missionary pastoral care, a position of fundamental importance is occupied even today, as in the past, by those people and institutions to whom the Decree Ad Gentes dedicates the chapter of the title: "Missionaries."128 In this regard, a deep reflection is necessary above all, for the missionaries themselves, who due to changes in the mission may feel inclined to no longer understand the meaning of their vocation, to no longer know what precisely the Church expects of them today.

66. Missionary Institutes, therefore, must use all the necessary resources, making available their experience and creativity with fidelity to the original charism, to adequately prepare the candidates and ensure the relief of the spiritual, moral and physical energies of their members.131 That they feel an active part of the ecclesial community and that they act in communion with it. In fact, «all religious Institutes were born by the Church and for her; their obligation is to enrich it with their own characteristics in accordance with its peculiar spirit and its specific mission" and the Bishops themselves are custodians of this fidelity to the charism that originated it.132

67. Collaborators of the Bishop, the priests, by virtue of the sacrament of Orders, are called to share the concern for the mission: « The spiritual gift that the priests received at ordination does not prepare them for a limited and restricted mission, but for the universal and very broad mission of salvation "to the ends of the earth", since any priestly ministry participates in the same universal breadth of the mission entrusted by Christ to the Apostles ".134 For this reason, the very formation of candidates for the priesthood must tend to give them "a genuinely Catholic spirit that accustoms them to looking beyond the limits of their own diocese, nation, rite and throwing themselves to the aid of the needs of the entire Church with a willingness to preach the Gospel everywhere." everything, to non-Christian groups in their own environment. May they feel in prayer and, particularly, in the Eucharistic sacrifice, the concern of the entire Church for all of humanity.

68. In the Encyclical Fidei donum, Pius XII, with prophetic intuition, encouraged the Bishops to offer some of their priests for temporary service to the Churches of Africa, approving the initiatives already existing in this regard. Twenty-five years later, I wanted to highlight the great novelty of that Document, which has overcome "the territorial dimension of priestly service to make it available to the entire Church."137 Today the validity and fruits of this experience are confirmed; In fact, the priests called Fidei donum highlight in a unique way the bond of communion between the Churches, they offer a valuable contribution to the growth of ecclesial communities in need, while finding freshness and vitality of faith in them. It is certainly necessary that the missionary service of the diocesan priest responds to some criteria and conditions. Priests must be sent chosen from among the best, suitable and duly prepared for the peculiar work that awaits them.138 They must be inserted into the new environment of the Church that receives them with an open and fraternal spirit, and they will constitute a single presbytery with the priests of the place, under the authority of the Bishop.139 My desire is that the spirit of service increases in the presbytery of the ancient Churches and that it be promoted in the presbytery of the older Churches. young people.

69. In the inexhaustible and multiform wealth of the Spirit are situated the vocations of the Institutes of consecrated life, whose members, "since by their very consecration they dedicate themselves to the service of the Church... are obliged to contribute in a special way to the missionary task, according to the proper way of their Institute."140 History bears witness to the great merits of religious Families in the propagation of the faith and in the formation of new Churches: from the ancient Institutions monastics, medieval Orders and even modern Congregations.

70. I want to address a few words of special gratitude to the missionary nuns, in whom virginity for the Kingdom is translated into multiple fruits of motherhood according to the spirit. Precisely the mission ad gentes offers them a vast field to "give themselves out of love in a total and undivided way."143 The example and industriousness of the virgin woman, consecrated to charity towards God and her neighbor, especially the poorest, are indispensable as an evangelical sign among those peoples and cultures in which women still have to make a long journey towards their human advancement and liberation. It is to be hoped that many young Christian women feel the attraction of giving themselves to Christ with generosity, finding in their consecration the strength and joy to bear witness to him among peoples who do not yet know him.

71. The Pontiffs of more recent times have insisted greatly on the importance of the role of the laity in missionary activity.144 In the Apostolic Exhortation Christifideles laici, I have also dealt explicitly with the "perennial mission of bringing the Gospel to those - and there are millions and millions of men and women - who do not yet know Christ the Redeemer of man,145 and with the corresponding responsibility of the lay faithful. The mission belongs to all the people of God: although the founding of a new Church requires the Eucharist and, consequently, the priestly ministry, nevertheless the mission, which is developed in various ways, is the task of all the faithful.

72. The sectors of presence and missionary action of the laity are very broad. «The proper field... is the vast and complex world of politics, social affairs, economics... »152 at the local, national and international level. Within the Church, various types of services, functions, ministries and forms of animation of Christian life are presented. I remember, as a novelty that has recently emerged in many Churches, the great development of "Ecclesial Movements", endowed with missionary dynamism. When they are humbly integrated into the life of local Churches and cordially welcomed by Bishops and priests in diocesan and parish structures, the Movements represent a true gift from God for the new evangelization and for missionary activity itself. Therefore, I recommend spreading them and using them to give new vigor, especially among young people, to Christian life and evangelization, with a pluralistic vision of the ways of associating and expressing themselves.

73. Among the lay people who become evangelizers, catechists are in the first line. The missionary conciliar Decree defines them as "that worthy legion of the work of missions among the Gentiles", who, "full of the apostolic spirit, provide with great sacrifices a singular and entirely necessary help for the expansion of the faith and the Church."154 Not without reason the oldest Churches, when dedicating themselves to a new evangelization, have increased the number of catechists and intensified catechesis. «The title of "catechist" is applied par excellence to catechists from mission lands... Without them flourishing Churches today would not have been built.»155

74. In addition to catechists, we must remember the other forms of service to the life of the Church and the mission, as well as other agents: animators of prayer, song and liturgy; responsible for base ecclesial communities and biblical groups; those in charge of charitable works; administrators of the property of the Church; leaders of the various apostolic groups and associations; religion teachers in schools. All lay faithful must dedicate part of their time to the Church, living their own faith coherently.

75. Those responsible and agents of missionary pastoral care must feel united in the communion that characterizes the mystical Body. For this reason Christ asked at the Last Supper: "As you, Father, are in me and I am in you, that they also may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me" (Jn 17, 21). In this communion lies the foundation of the fruitfulness of the mission.

76. For the orientation and coordination of missionary activity at the national and regional level, the Episcopal Conferences and their various groups are of great importance. The Council asks them to "deal..., by common agreement, with the most serious issues and the most urgent problems, but without neglecting local differences,"162 as well as the problem of inculturation. In fact, there is already extensive and continued action in this field and the fruits are visible. It is an action that must be intensified and better coordinated with that of other organizations of the same Conferences, so that the missionary request is not reduced to the direction of a certain sector or organization, but is shared by all.

77. Members of the Church by virtue of baptism, all Christians are co-responsible for missionary activity. The participation of the communities and of each faithful in this right-duty is called "missionary cooperation."

78. Among the forms of participation, the first place corresponds to spiritual cooperation: prayer, sacrifices, testimony of Christian life. Prayer must accompany the path of missionaries, so that the announcement of the Word is effective through divine grace. Saint Paul, in his Letters, often asks the faithful to pray for him, so that he can announce the Gospel with confidence and frankness.

79. Cooperation is also manifested in promoting missionary vocations. In this regard, the validity of the various forms of missionary activity must be recognized; but, at the same time, it is necessary to reaffirm the priority of total and perpetual donation to the work of the missions, especially in the missionary Institutes and Congregations, male and female. The promotion of these vocations is the heart of cooperation: the proclamation of the Gospel requires announcers, the harvest needs workers, the mission is carried out, above all, with men and women consecrated for life to the work of the Gospel, willing to go throughout the world to bring salvation.

80. Thinking about this serious problem, I address my call, with particular confidence and affection, to families and young people. Families and, above all, parents must be aware that they must make "a particular contribution to the missionary cause of the Church, cultivating missionary vocations among their sons and daughters."167

81. The material and economic needs of the missions are many; not only to found the Church with minimal structures (capillas, escuelas para catequistas y seminaristas, viviendas), but also to sustain works of charity, education and human promotion, an immense field of action, especially in poor countries. The missionary Church gives what it receives; He distributes to the poor what his wealthiest children in material resources generously put at their disposal. In this regard, I wish to thank all those who give sacrificially for missionary work; Their renunciations and participation are essential to build the Church and witness to charity.

referencias.descripcion: capillas, escuelas para catequistas y seminaristas, viviendas

contenido: 82. Cooperation today opens up to new forms, including not only economic aid but also direct participation. New situations related to the phenomenon of human mobility demand from Christians an authentic missionary spirit.

83. The missionary formation of the People of God is the work of the local Church with the help of the missionaries and their Institutes, as well as the members of the young Churches. This work must be understood not as something marginal, but central in the Christian life. For the same "new evangelization" of Christian peoples, the missionary theme can be of great help: in fact, the testimony of missionaries retains its attractiveness even for those who are distant and non-believers, and is a transmitter of Christian values. Local Churches, therefore, must include missionary animation as a primary element of their ordinary pastoral care in parishes, associations and groups, especially youth groups.

84. In this work of animation the primary task corresponds to the Pontifical Mission Societies, as I have stated several times in the Messages for World Mission Day. The four Works – Propagation of the Faith, Saint Peter the Apostle, Holy Childhood and Missionary Union – have in common the objective of promoting the universal missionary spirit in the People of God. The Missionary Union's immediate and specific purpose is to raise awareness and missionary formation of priests, men and women religious who, in turn, must cultivate it in Christian communities; Furthermore, it tries to promote other Works, of which it is the soul.168 "The motto must be this: All the Churches for the conversion of the whole world."169 These Works, being of the Pope and the Episcopal College, even in the scope of the particular Churches, "must rightfully occupy the first place, since they are means to spread among Catholics, from childhood, the truly universal and missionary meaning, and to stimulate the effective collection of subsidies in favor of all the missions , according to the needs of each one. "170 Another objective of the Missionary Works is to raise vocations ad gentes and for life, both in the ancient Churches and in the younger ones. I strongly recommend that your entertainment service be increasingly oriented towards this end.

85. Cooperating with the missions means not only giving, but also knowing how to receive: all particular Churches, young or old, are called to give and receive in favor of the universal mission and none should close themselves in on themselves: "By virtue of this catholicity," says the Council, "each of the parts collaborates with its own gifts with the remaining parts and with the entire Church, in such a way that the whole and each of the parts increase because of all those that mutually communicate and tend to plenitude in unity... From this are derived... between the various parts of the Church, ties of intimate communion with regard to spiritual riches, apostolic workers and temporal help. "171

86. If we look superficially at our world, many negative facts are striking that can lead to pessimism. But this is an unjustified feeling: we have faith in God the Father and Lord, in his goodness and mercy. As the third millennium of the Redemption approaches, God is preparing a great Christian spring, the beginning of which is already in sight. Indeed, both in the non-Christian world and in that of ancient Christian tradition, there is a progressive approach of people to the ideals and evangelical values, which the Church strives to promote. Today a new convergence of people towards these values ​​is manifested: the rejection of violence and war; respect for the human person and their rights; the desire for freedom, justice and fraternity; the tendency to overcome racism and nationalism; the strengthening of the dignity and appreciation of women.
87. Missionary activity requires a specific spirituality, which particularly concerns those who God has called to be missionaries.

88. An essential note of missionary spirituality is intimate communion with Christ: the mission cannot be understood and lived if it is not with reference to Christ, as sent to evangelize. Paul describes their attitudes: “Have among yourselves the same sentiments as Christ: Who, being divine in form, did not greedily regard equality with God. But he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and appearing in appearance like a man; and he humbled himself, obeying even unto death, even death on a cross" (Flp 2, 5-8).

89. Missionary spirituality is also characterized by apostolic charity; that of Christ who came "to gather into one the children of God who were scattered" (Jn 11, 52); Christ, Good Shepherd who knows his sheep, seeks them and offers his life for them (cf. Jn 10). Whoever has a missionary spirit feels the ardor of Christ for souls and loves the Church, like Christ.

90. The call to mission derives in itself from the call to holiness. Each missionary is authentically so if he strives on the path of holiness: "Holiness is a fundamental presupposition and an irreplaceable condition for carrying out the saving mission of the Church."174

91. I address myself, therefore, to the baptized of the young communities and the young Churches. Today you are the hope of our Church, which is two thousand years old: being young in the faith, you must be like the first Christians and radiate enthusiasm and courage, with generous dedication to God and your neighbor; In a word, you must take the path of holiness. Only in this way can you be signs of God in the world and revive in your countries the missionary epic of the early Church. And you will also be a leaven of missionary spirit for the oldest Churches.

92. Never has the Church had the opportunity like today to make the Gospel reach, with testimony and word, to all men and all peoples. I see the dawn of a new missionary era, which will become a day radiant and rich in fruits, if all Christians and, in particular, missionaries and young Churches respond with generosity and holiness to the requests and challenges of our time. Like the Apostles after the Ascension of Christ, the Church must meet in the Upper Room with "Mary, the mother of Jesus" (Act 1, 14), to implore the Spirit and obtain strength and courage to fulfill the missionary mandate. We too, much more than the Apostles, need to be transformed and guided by the Spirit.
